purpose: Reading platter for interface persuasion: how color, position, labels and defaults steer a choice among priced options, and how strong the evidence for each is. Opened for a study of pricing-tier color.
posture: Index and citation only. No source text or page image is reproduced; short quotations only, source named.

checked_key.true: citation details confirmed against a publisher, repository or catalog record during a platter pass
checked_key.false: some detail (authors, pages, sample size or title) written from working knowledge or a secondary source; wants a verification pass before it is cited in a paper

shelves.attention: Where the eye goes while choosing: salience, size, position, order.
shelves.color: What hue, saturation and lightness do to price perception and choice, with the replications and reversals.
shelves.choice: Labels, defaults, decoys and dark patterns: steering among priced options, measured on real purchases where possible.
shelves.practice: Practitioner tests and counts of pricing pages. Lower-grade evidence, labelled as such.
shelves.regulation: Where visual steering becomes a deceptive practice.
shelves.access: Contrast and color-vision limits any palette must meet.

sources.title: The visual environment and attention in decision making
sources.why: Meta-analysis of 122 effect sizes on where people look while choosing. Central position ρ = .43, surface size ρ = .35, visual salience ρ = .13. The outcome is gaze, not purchase. The strongest single source for 'position and size beat salience'.

sources.title: Attention and choice: A review on eye movements in decision making
sources.why: Narrative review of eye movements in decision making; concludes no theory fully accounts for the role of attention.

sources.title: Relative visual saliency differences induce sizable bias in consumer choice
sources.why: Three lab food-choice experiments. Salience was set by local brightness, not hue; the bias appears under fast decisions, cognitive load and weak preferences. Sample sizes and effect size not confirmed at source.

sources.title: The subtlety of distinctiveness: What von Restorff really did
sources.why: The isolation effect is a memory advantage for the odd item in a list. Applying it to which plan gets bought is extrapolation.

sources.title: Position-based beliefs: The center-stage effect
sources.why: People believe the middle option in a row is the popular one and choose it more. The mechanism is inferred popularity, not attention.

sources.title: Shining in the center: Central gaze cascade effect on product choice
sources.why: Eye-tracking: horizontally central brands get more attention and are chosen more.

sources.title: Position effects in choice from simultaneous displays: A conundrum solved
sources.why: Review: middle bias is the most common position effect, but first and last advantages also occur.

sources.title: The influence of price presentation order on consumer choice
sources.why: Descending price order steers toward pricier options. One paper; sample sizes not retrieved.

sources.title: Are men seduced by red? The effect of red versus black prices on price perceptions
sources.why: Red prices raised perceived savings for men under low involvement only. No independent replication found.

sources.title: Red price? Red flag! Eye-tracking reveals how one red price can hurt a retailer
sources.why: One red price among others lowered perceived savings: the reverse of the folk reading of Puccinelli 2013.

sources.title: Visual finance: The pervasive effects of red on investor behavior
sources.why: Eight experiments: red on financial data signals loss and lowers risk-taking. Absent in colorblind participants, muted in China, not explained by salience.

sources.title: The effect of red background color on willingness-to-pay: The moderating role of selling mechanism
sources.why: Red raised bids in auctions and lowered offers in negotiations. Fixed-price purchase was not tested.

sources.title: Exciting red and competent blue: The importance of color in marketing
sources.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 40, 711–727. DOI 10.1007/s11747-010-0245-y
sources.why: Hue mapped to brand-personality ratings of invented logos. Association data, not behavior.

sources.title: Color psychology: Effects of perceiving color on psychological functioning in humans
sources.why: Color-in-context theory. The authors call the literature 'at a nascent stage'. DOI added from working knowledge.

sources.title: Failure to replicate the Mehta and Zhu (2009) color-priming effect on anagram solution times
sources.why: Direct replication with more than three times the sample found no red-versus-blue effect. Title and pages from working knowledge.

sources.title: Limited evidence for the effect of red color on cognitive performance: A meta-analysis
sources.why: 67 effect sizes: no evidential value for red and performance after publication-bias correction.

sources.title: Color saturation increases perceived product size
sources.why: Six experiments: higher saturation raises perceived size through arousal and attention. Supports 'saturation, not hue, carries weight'. Volume and pages from working knowledge.

sources.title: Universal patterns in color-emotion associations are further shaped by linguistic and geographic proximity
sources.why: 4,598 participants in 30 nations: color–emotion associations are largely shared (r = .88). Red is the main exception.

sources.title: Observational learning: Evidence from a randomized natural field experiment
sources.why: Showing a restaurant's five most popular dishes raised demand for them by 13–18%; merely listing dishes did less. Separates learning from others from salience.

sources.title: The influence of food recommendations: Evidence from a randomized field experiment
sources.why: A 'most popular' label raised selection by about 13%; an expert label did not. Published title not confirmed.

sources.title: When and why defaults influence decisions: A meta-analysis of default effects
sources.why: 58 studies, N = 73,675, d = 0.68. Stronger when the default reads as an endorsement.

sources.title: The limits of attraction
sources.why: 19 studies with realistic stimuli; no decoy effect in any.

sources.title: The compromise effect in action: Lessons from a restaurant's menu
sources.venue: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization 128, 14–34. DOI 10.1016/j.jebo.2016.04.017
sources.why: More than 88,000 real choices: an option that becomes the compromise gains about five points of share; not significant for people ordering alone.

sources.title: Shining a light on dark patterns
sources.why: Mild dark patterns roughly doubled uptake of a paid plan without backlash; aggressive ones caused backlash.

sources.title: The effects of highlighting a recommended pricing plan (original research)
sources.why: The one study that isolates a highlighted plan: fixated sooner (p = .0171, cheap-first order) and chosen more often. Hypothetical choices, one product, sample sizes shown only in images, not replicated.

sources.title: Visual hierarchy in UX: Definition
sources.why: Hierarchy comes from contrast in value and saturation between an element and its context, not from the hue. Year approximate.

sources.title: SaaS pricing page examples
sources.why: 245 pages: 16% carry a 'most popular' or 'best value' text label (a floor); 18% price in credits, and 15 of the 34 pages added since January 2025 do.

sources.title: 'Most popular' badge prevalence on pricing pages
sources.why: 38% of 301 detected pricing experiments mention a recommended-plan badge; keyword lower bound over model-written text.

sources.title: SaaS pricing pages: a study of the Montclare SaaS 250
sources.why: 48 pages with public pricing: half highlight one package; four packages most common.

sources.title: Pricing screen A/B tests
sources.why: Live tests on pricing badges and price type size. Both readable entries have under 35% power at a 5% effect, and results sit behind a membership wall.

sources.title: Bringing dark patterns to light (staff report)
sources.why: Appendix A names 'False Hierarchy': contrasting visual prominence used to steer a selection.

sources.title: Digital Services Act, Article 25 (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065)
sources.venue: Official Journal of the European Union
sources.why: Online platforms may not design interfaces that deceive or manipulate; guidance may address 'giving more prominence to certain choices'. Read from a text mirror, not EUR-Lex.

sources.title: Online choice architecture: How digital design can harm competition and consumers (CMA155)
sources.why: Choice architecture is a neutral term; it harms when visual features or popularity claims mislead.

sources.title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2
sources.why: 1.4.3 text contrast 4.5:1, 1.4.11 non-text contrast 3:1, 1.4.1 color is not the only signal.

sources.title: Worldwide prevalence of red-green color deficiency
sources.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A 29(3), 313–320
sources.why: Red–green deficiency in about 8% of men and 0.4% of women of European descent.
